I'm not really sure how to start talking about this game. I guess I'll start by saying that the only Forza games I've played are Horizon 1 and 5. I emulated 1, and then jumped to 5 because it was the only one on steam (sidenote, delisting games is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥). Maybe my opinion of this game would be less favorable had I played 2-4 first, because the biggest complaint I hear about 5 is that it doesn't make any meaningful improvements to the formula. It's just the same thing again with a new coat of paint, except it does some things worse than previous games. This could be 100% true. Hell, there are some things that I think Horizon 1 does better, like your progression through the festival and the general vibe. 5 feels very sanitized and simplified. You start at the top, you're showered with rewards, everyone calls you "superstar" constantly and feel like they're only there to hype you up. None of the attitude of the rivals in 1. Races are open to all performance classes and car types, so the game never pushes you to try new things. There's no sense of working your way towards anything; you just kinda pick whatever events you feel like doing until the whole festival is unlocked. It didn't help that I got the deluxe edition, so the game gave me a ton of high performance cars before I even did anything. I would even argue that the soundtrack in 1 is better, even though there are some bangers in 5. But with all that said, I did still put 200 hours into the game, so clearly they did SOMETHING right. I think what I've concluded is that while it may not have any standout features, it isn't really bad at any of the things you can do. Racing is still fun. Cars control very nicely, and there's a large selection of cool cars to get. Taking a drive around the map is very nice. EventLab is full of cool ♥♥♥♥ that other people have made. I don't know, it's just fun. It's kinda become my comfort game. So if you're a diehard forza fan, I totally see how it could be disappointing. But if you're not and you just want a quality open world racing game to sink some time into, go for it. Unless Horizon 6 is better. I wouldn't know, I haven't played it yet.

In a vacuum, this is a *great* racing game. Unfortunately for Forza Horizon 5, it doesn't exist in a vacuum; it exists alongside other Forza Horizon games. The only timeframe where this game became reasonably good was between December 15, 2024 (with the delisting of Forza Horizon 4), and May 16, 2026 (with the release of Forza Horizon 6). Between those two games in the series, I struggle to think of a single thing that Forza Horizon 5 actually did better. Sure, the cars look and sound great, but this game is just missing the *soul* that other games in the series have had. I'm willing to extend a lot of grace to Playground Games, what with this game being developed during a global pandemic and all, but at some point you have to draw a line in the sand and recognize that this entry just does not live up to the standards set by the series. For starters, the music. Now, I realize that this is purely subjective on my part, but I feel like FH5 is sorely lacking in the soundtrack department. Every song felt middling at best, and failed to capture the energy of Horizon Mexico other than a couple of Spanish covers of pop songs. I also understand that people are divided on the in-game DJs, but if it weren't for the iconic energy brought by Scott Tyler and Amy Simpson, I would have very little reason to listen to radio at all (skill songs not withstanding). Secondly, as other have pointed out, progression is completely non-existent in this game. I'm not going to beat the dead horse found in dozens of other comments, but suffice it to say that building out the festival via accolades did not feel the least bit meaningful. To make matters worse, accolades become nearly pointless after completing the festival aside from being used as a ranking metric among clans. But finally, and perhaps most egregiously, was the controversial opinion to finally make your character have voice lines. Now look, I know there are running jokes about silent protagonists from dozens of other game series, but the lines and delivery from the main character are a joke in and of itself. I would never talk like that, I would never say any of the corny one-liners that are delivered time and time again by your character. The fact that your only voice options are two different flavors of British are the real nail in the coffin for putting yourself in the festival Superstar's shoes. All in all, there was no reason to jump on this entry while Forza Horizon 4 was around, and now that Forza Horizon 6 is here, I imagine that this particular low point in the series will fade into obscurity where it belongs.

Still vastly superior to Forza Horizon 6. While some say the map in Forza Horizon 5 feels bland, it still offers something the latest installment does not: lots of fun in free roam mode. Whether you're just looking to cruise, or cause some mayhem, there is always some place to go. The map itself offers some unique scenery too, from azure beaches to a jungle airstrip amidst old Mayan ruins, to a volcano and a long meandering canyon. The variety in Horizon 5 is still vast if you're actually willing to explore the map past the Dunas Blancas.  Sure, it might not be its British predecessor, which features an astonishing map with great use of the seasons (Horizon 5 not so much). But the road network is incredibly well thought out, and if that's your thing, you can reach a high-speed flow almost anywhere on the map; unlike that newest installment which seems to be littered with trees, ditches, and hills that hamper any fun. That coupled with a central highway that you will actually use, makes it a lot of fun to try out your latest hypercar.  The best part about Horizon 5, though, is the racing. Horizon 5 features lots of memorable tracks. Returning to this installment from Horizon 6 made me realize how much I missed the intelligent race track design in this installment. Whether it is the Bola Ocho Circuit, the Mulegé Town Scramble, or the Panorámica Sprint, almost all race tracks feature intelligent race design, tight corners, and thrilling action, whether it's solo or co-op.  The Horizon Festival and the Horizon Adventure, with its many Horizon Outposts, also make the map feel alive and give you a great place to stop and tinker with your car. All in all, it's a shame this game will get retired. Forza Horizon 5 gave and still gives me a lot of fun, whereas I'm already tired of the bland, vast emptiness of Japan. Sure, there is a lot of detail in the Forza Horizon 6 map, but it is detail you never see because you will never be cruising around the map just for fun. Forza Horizon 5, however, invites you to go pedal to the metal and have some fun all the time.

🏆 The Ultimate Sandbox Racing Masterpiece Overall Rating: 9.5/10 (Highly Recommended)  Forza Horizon 5 remains the gold standard for open-world arcade-sim racing. Playground Games has crafted a stunning digital rendition of Mexico that is as much a love letter to car culture as it is an exhilarating sandbox game. Whether you are casually cruising in a supercar or tuning a drift beast for competitive rivals, the game delivers on every front.  🏎️ Visuals & Sound Design Next-Gen Graphics: The biomes—ranging from the active caldera volcano to dense, living jungles and pristine beaches—are breathtaking. Photogrammetry technology brings every rock, cactus, and asphalt texture to life.  Audio Engine: A massive leap forward from previous titles. Engine notes sound distinct, raw, and highly responsive to modifications (exhaust, turbos, superchargers). The dynamic spatial audio changes realistically depending on whether you are driving through a canyon or an open field.  🕹️ Gameplay & Physics Mechanics The Perfect Hybrid ("Sim-Cade"): The physics engine strikes a brilliant balance. It is accessible enough for controller players to jump in and pick up immediate speed, yet nuanced enough to reward proper braking lines, weight transfer management, and throttle control.  Peripheral & Wheel Support: The game shines on a controller, but it has also significantly improved force feedback dynamics for racing wheel setups compared to its predecessor. Setting up a dedicated wheel configuration with software like x360ce or Hid Hide yields a highly immersive, responsive driving experience once dialed in.  Car List & Customization: With hundreds of meticulously detailed vehicles, the progression feels incredibly rewarding. The tuning system is incredibly deep, allowing you to tweak gear ratios, tire pressure, differential lock, and suspension geometry down to the finest detail.  🖥️ Performance & Technical Optimization Scalability: The PC port is incredibly well-optimized. Even on mid-range hardware (such as an i5 paired with an RTX 3060 class GPU), the game scales beautifully, delivering a locked, high-framerate experience at 1080p/1440p High-Ultra settings with robust thermal stability.  Loading Times: Optimized perfectly for SSDs, making fast-travel and swapping between your massive garage seamless.  💬 Final Verdict Forza Horizon 5 is an absolute must-own for anyone with even a passing interest in cars. It successfully removes the stress of rigid track simulators while keeping the depth that makes driving mechanics fun. It isn't just a racing game; it’s a massive festival celebration of automotive freedom.  Pros:  Breathtaking world design and weather effects.  Impeccable PC optimization and stable framerates.  Deep mechanical tuning that actually alters vehicle handling.  Cons:  The UI menus can occasionally feel cluttered due to the sheer volume of content.  Online Horizon Life servers can occasionally experience minor sync hiccups during peak hours.

After spending 257 hours in Mexico and driving more than 250 different cars, I can confidently say that Forza Horizon 5 gave me one of the most complete open-world racing experiences I've ever had.  The map of Mexico is fascinating. From driving off-road deep inside dense jungles while discovering ancient ruins, to finding crystal-clear rivers and hidden waterfalls, climbing a massive volcano, or simply taking a beautiful coupe for a relaxing drive along the beach at sunset... every trip feels different.  Although I still believe Britain in Forza Horizon 4 had a more memorable atmosphere, Mexico offers something different. It isn't as charming as London, but it's much larger, more diverse, and full of hidden places that constantly reward exploration. Every time I thought I had seen everything, I found another beautiful road, another forgotten village, or another amazing landscape waiting for me.  Graphically, Playground Games once again proved why this series stands above most open-world racing games. Every new Horizon feels more polished and more mature than the previous one. The lighting, weather effects, vegetation, and environmental details create an incredible driving experience.  The cars are beautifully designed, feel realistic to drive, and never feel artificial. The variety is outstanding—no matter what type of driver you are, there is always a car that fits your style. On top of that, the upgrade and tuning systems remain one of the strongest features of the franchise. Being able to fine-tune every part of a car and actually feel the difference is something many racing games still fail to deliver.  Vehicle sounds have improved noticeably compared to the previous game. However, I still think engine swaps need more work. Sometimes installing a V10 makes completely different cars sound almost identical, which takes away some of their unique personality.  My favorite part of the game is the amount of variety it offers. A huge map, different race types, changing weather, seasonal events, and even unexpected sandstorms that suddenly appear and completely change your visibility—it constantly finds new ways to surprise you and keep every drive interesting.  My Score  Graphics: 8.5/10 Map Design: 8/10 Driving Physics: 9/10 Sound Design: 8.5/10 Content Variety: 8/10 Progression: 7.5/10  Overall: 8/10  Final Verdict  Forza Horizon 5 isn't perfect, but after more than 250 hours, I never felt like I was forcing myself to play. I simply enjoyed getting behind the wheel, exploring new roads, trying different cars, and creating my own journey.  Some games are made to be finished. Forza Horizon 5 is made to be driven.

A fun racer with a big map and a ton to do, Forza Horizon 5 succeeds in succeeds in having exciting races and a surprising variety of content for a strictly car-based game, but also suffers from a few roadblocks which are partly personal for me but also partly from design.  This is Forza, so you know the racing is good; I'm not really much of a gearhead so I don't know a ton about cars, meaning I stuck with the starting Corvette for the vast majority of my 15 hours with this game, which I feel a little bad about because from what I can tell there are over 900 vehicles in this thing, which is absolutely absurd! I bet for someone who knows their motors this is an absolute treat, and I can imagine it feels awesome being able to drive a "dream car" and use them in pretty much any race you want, as well as utilising all the tuning and customisation options that the game gives you. Unfortunately for someone who's not so familiar with this kind of stuff, I feel like the game doesn't make much of an effort to onboard you at all with what each category of car does, what certain stats mean, or how to change certain specific traits of car (I wanted to try a Camaro at one point, but I hated the steering; I'm sure there's a way to change how it handles but I didn't know what to look at when it came to the tuning menu!) these issues are compounded by the absolutely horrendous UI which just stacks menus on top of menus inside of tabs which you find through other menus; this ridiculous level of menuing combined with pretty regular loading times relating to buying vehicles led me to be very very disincentivized from purchasing any cars at all really, which kinda sucks! This lack of onboarding also extends to some of the driving itself; I get that this is the 5th game in the Horizon series, so they probably don't want to Pokémon this ♥♥♥♥, but at least some sort of option for "would you like a tutorial on how to drift?" would have been amazing; as it stands I could not get a handle on the e-drifting at all in this game, I'd just hit A and my car's handling would completely ♥♥♥♥ itself.  Anyways, with the majority of my problems out of the way, there is tons to actually enjoy here! The sheer variety of stuff this game manages to pack in despite its restrictions of being "just a driving game" is very impressive; the most notable of these is the big Showcase Events, which are usually a setpiece race against a unique opponent like planes, trains, or jetskis! These are all really cool and fun and I was always looking forward to unlocking more of them. Unfortunately they don't all hit (one of them just unlocks a series of 1v1 races which is a bit disappointing) but the level of success I'd say on them is at least 70%. This game is also very pretty to look at; Mexico is a cool region to drive around (even though I do personally find desert biomes pretty boring) with some a bit of variety to stop it from feeling too samey; beaches, jungles, and some really beautiful towns are mainly what you'll see when you're not racing on highways through the desert, and the towns especially are gorgeous, I love the architecture and particularly the splash of colour it brings to these otherwise quite brown and yellow environments.  The bottom line is this is an enjoyable open world racer that will only get more enjoyable the more you know about cars and racing. Even as someone who's not super familiar with these things I'd say this is still pretty damn good! 7/10

When I'm craving some stylish racing challenges, or just want to zoom around feeling like a badass in a super fast well-controlled car, Forza 5 absolutely delivers! This game is such a beautiful playground for car racing, of so many varieties, with so many awesome models of cars tossed at your finger tips!  It's neat how it branches from the typical model of tuning your own cars, to allow you to use community designs and tuning builds, to quickly get a nice setup for your favorite car styles, without having to spend lots of time on your own custom setup. Of course its great that they still let you do your own customizations too.  It's also cool how the AI tends to scale around the current build of the car you choose to drive. Plus there is so many adjustments to difficulty one can make, in how their car performs, and how tough the AI are, to keep most of the gameplay within a desired difficulty range.  My only caveats are that the community builds that you choose are locked once chosen, with so much of the build information no longer shown to you after spending credits on that build. But I feel like this is a minor issue, in this arcadey style many-type racing playground; because while you can't see some of the stats most of the time, you can still absolutely feel them after the tuning changes.

Forza Horizon 5 made me fall in love with Mexico so hard that I now want to visit it in real life. Deserts, jungles, beaches, volcanoes — basically a travel ad, but with 900 cars and a much higher chance of crashing into a cactus.  My friend and I have been playing since launch back in 2021, and somehow we still haven’t collected all the bonus boards. Some of them are hidden like government secrets. I know I could just look them up online, but at that point my pride gets involved, and my pride is apparently worse at navigation than the GPS.  So yes, if you want to collect every board, the Treasure Map might be less of a DLC and more of a mental health service.  I honestly think this part felt even more fun than Horizon 4, maybe because Mexico is so bright, warm and full of life. It’s sad to leave it behind now that the next Horizon is here — especially because keeping both games installed would require deleting half my SSD and possibly several personal memories.  At the end of the day, it’s Forza: cars go fast, scenery looks illegally beautiful, and your garage slowly becomes a psychological condition.  10/10 — came for racing, stayed for Mexico, still looking for that one stupid board.

After nearly 400 hours in Forza Horizon 5, I can safely say this is one of the best arcade racing games ever made.  What started as "I'll have a quick drive around Mexico" turned into an obsession to collect every car in the game. Hundreds of hours later, I was still finding reasons to log in each week, complete seasonal challenges, hunt down rare vehicles, and add another car to the garage.  The map is fantastic, offering everything from deserts and jungles to mountain roads and coastal highways. Whether you're drifting, racing, off-roading, cruising, or simply exploring, there's always something to do and somewhere new to drive.  The car selection is absolutely ridiculous in the best possible way. Hypercars, classics, rally legends, hot hatches, muscle cars, off-road monsters, obscure oddities – if you're a car enthusiast, there's a good chance your dream garage exists somewhere in this game. Collecting them all became a game within the game for me.  What really kept me coming back was the seasonal content. The weekly Festival Playlist gives you a reason to keep playing long after the main campaign is complete, and unlocking rare cars feels genuinely rewarding. Some of my proudest gaming moments involved finally tracking down the last few elusive vehicles for the collection.  The driving strikes a near-perfect balance between arcade fun and realism. It's easy to pick up, difficult to master, and somehow manages to make almost every car feel enjoyable to drive.  Visually, it's stunning. Even after hundreds of hours, I still find myself taking the long route to an event just because the game looks so good. The weather effects, lighting, and vehicle detail are among the best in the genre.  No game is perfect. Some cars being locked behind limited-time events can be frustrating, especially for new players trying to complete their collection. But the developers have continued supporting the game with new content, cars, features and events long after launch, helping to keep the community active and the game feeling fresh.  The biggest compliment I can give Forza Horizon 5 is this: after nearly 400 hours, I was still logging in because I wanted to, not because I felt I had to.  If you enjoy cars, open-world games, collecting, racing, or simply driving for the sake of driving, this is an easy recommendation.  Now if you'll excuse me, I'm just checking the Festival Playlist to see if I'm missing another car...

Ah yes, good cars, cringy voice lines: the game.  The worst thing about Forza is when any character talks.  You are my superstar, amigo.  My wife’s boyfriend says it’s a game to enjoy cars and drive them freely on an open map with beatiful landscapes.   I on the other hand play it to "drive" all my favorite cars that I'll never be able to afford like a complete lunatic across the country.   You can actually FEEL yourself riding over the Horizon.  The cars sound better than FH4 and FH6. ‘Nough said.   I mean, what else can I say? To my autistic mind, the cars going vroom just make me happy.  It’s a game that will finally be loved now that FH6 is out.  It’s literally THE BEST open world racing game ever made. Every single second of Forza Horizon 5 feels like an episode of Top Gear. It's an absolute dream for anyone with even a passing interest in vehicles, and the closest thing to heaven for any and all gearheads.   Forza Horizon is a very "vibe" kind of game. The whole goal of the game is to drive your favorite cars in a beautiful sandbox type world. If you just want a game to play and have fun without thinking about mechanics, progression, story or anything really, you can always just launch the game and have fun. I think the Forza Horizon games have always had that perfect balance between simulation and arcade lunacy. And damn, does the game look gorgeous. Seriously, the graphic's are more realistic than my eyes! There aren't many other driving games that have the same variety and scope, and hit a great balance between casual and more competitive play.   Tbh as I’ve gotten older I’ve stopped caring for track racing or chasing times, so I just enjoy cruising around in these types of games. And for me, no other open world game touches the physics and overall driving feel of FH. I’ve tried the crew and the newer NFS games, and while they do some things well, the actual feel of the driving is still so lackluster in comparison. The way it feels to drive cars is just absolutely dialed in to the finest degree. It's insanely hard to go to another racer after being spoiled by how nice Horizon has become. Some car games will do graphics a bit sharper, or sounds a bit better here or there, but as an overall package Horizon 5 is absolutely unmatched. ESPECIALLY on controller. There is no legit comparison to how crisp the quality of control the game has when you put it up against ALL of its peers.  I like everything about it! I can adjust the difficulty so my disabled child can play and not get frustrated. The representation in character design makes me happy. There are so many different things to do. The driving feels fantastic. The cars feel great to drive in that arcadey but still weighty feel. Cars have an identity to them so you can really choose what you think fits best for a certain type of track. I loved collecting new cars and finding my next favourite. The tracks were mostly good and fun to drive through. The attention to detail in the cars and their look is above others in the genre, by a mile. I've been playing The Crew 2 recently and there's just no competition in the way cars handle, sound and look.  The game is meant to be a celebration of all things cars through the guise of a festival. You start at the main hub, central festival location and build your way through more Festival Outposts. Each Outpost is colored towards one of the before mentioned race event types. Doing the races associated with that Outpost will unlock another small story that usually concludes with a large, set piece race themed towards those events. It allows you to customize and earn rewards for almost every action you do in game. The money earned in game is then spent on cosmetic items for your character, cars, or upgrades on those vehicles. The upgrade system lets you go as deep as you really want to go for improving your performance. Build your own dream machine, tune it to really dial in the performance, or download someone else's tune for the car.  All in all, Forza Horizon is just pure fun for those who hold a love of all things cars. If you have ever watched Top Gear, this is essentially the type of tone the game sets for how it treats all its 815 unique cars in the game. If you appreciate racing games and being able to drive and do the things you want to do, this is a game for you. I mean, for real, what's not to like? It's got every darn thing you could want: variety of races, open world, challenges between real players, group events, map editor, custom races, weekly and monthly challenges, story mode, hot wheels world, off road world, customizing cars, cars galore, fine tuned difficulty settings, multiple points of view, and on and on. It gives you an overall freedom of doing whatever your heart desires. Seriously, the only limits there are your creativity and skills. I highly recommend it.  9/10

The game plays how any other FH game would, it seems they don't really change the gameplay aspect, rather than just quality of life changes and the main premise of the story. 5 taking place in Mexico was honestly a breath of fresh air, London felt very cluttered and crowded so being able to take in the beautiful landscape of Mexico was a nice change of pace. The car selection is great as always, with easter eggs like the Halo warthog and such; also featuring my favorite car, the Nissan 350z (2002). The story was...fine, I guess? The voice acting was horrible but I do like how the narrator says your name, I thought that was cool and to be frank I can't remember if it was in the previous titles. I really liked the Donut missions, as I used to watch Donut a lot and it was fun to play missions that correlated to some of their videos (like Hi and Low). Top Gear is always a banger mission arc as well. It's kinda relaxing going around to find all of the pinatas and smash xp boards and such, a classic Horizon feature. The DLCs were sort of mid, like the Hot Wheels one was ok and I actually thought the map was pretty cool with the seasons and such, but the other DLC with the teams was boring, I didn't even finish it. “Bigger map, brighter world, same incredible driving fun.”  Forza Horizon 5 takes everything great about the series and pushes it into a more vibrant, more diverse, and more visually impressive direction. Set in a stunning recreation of Mexico, the game immediately stands out with its color, scale, and environmental variety.  The world design is easily one of its biggest strengths. From dense jungles and sandy deserts to volcanic peaks and lively cities, every region feels distinct and worth exploring. The dynamic weather system and seasonal events add extra life without overwhelming the experience.  Driving feels as smooth and satisfying as ever. The handling is accessible but still rewarding, striking a nice balance between arcade fun and light realism. Whether you’re racing competitively, drifting for style points, or just cruising around, the game consistently feels good to play.  There’s also an overwhelming amount of content. Events, stories, online modes, seasonal playlists, and car collections ensure there’s always something to chase. It’s the kind of game you can drop into for 20 minutes or lose an entire evening in without realizing.  However, compared to its predecessor, the core gameplay loop doesn’t feel dramatically different. It’s more of an evolution than a revolution. Some players may also find the progression a bit too relaxed, and online stability can occasionally be inconsistent.  Pros:  Stunning and diverse open world Extremely smooth and fun driving mechanics Huge amount of content and events Excellent visual presentation  Cons:  Feels similar to FH4 in core structure Progression can feel too easy Occasional online/server issues  Verdict: A visually spectacular and consistently fun racing experience. It doesn’t reinvent the formula, but it absolutely perfects it.  Highly Recommended 👍

Titlu: Festivalul Suprem al Vitezei – Forza Horizon 5  ★★★★★ Recomand  Forza Horizon 5 este genul de joc care îți amintește de ce iubim mașinile. Nu doar pentru viteză, ci pentru libertate. Playground Games a luat formula deja aproape perfectă din Horizon 4 și a împins-o într-o nouă ligă: o lume gigantică, mai vie, mai diversă și mai spectaculoasă decât orice alt joc arcade racing de pe piață.  Atmosferă și Lume  Mexicul din Forza Horizon 5 este absolut superb. De la jungle tropicale și deșerturi imense până la orașe colorate, vulcani activi și furtuni de nisip, fiecare zonă are personalitate proprie. Jocul nu doar că arată bine — respiră viață. Cerul, lumina, ploaia, reflexiile pe mașini… uneori uiți că te joci și ai impresia că vezi reclame auto de milioane de dolari.  Festivalul Horizon păstrează vibe-ul acela energic și relaxat: muzică, petreceri, curse nebune și sentimentul că întreaga lume e construită pentru distracție pură.  Gameplay  Aici jocul domină aproape complet competiția arcade. Condusul este accesibil pentru oricine, dar suficient de profund încât să simți diferența dintre o mașină AWD, RWD sau un monstru hypercar de 1500 cai.  Fiecare mașină are greutate, personalitate și sunet propriu. Sistemul de tuning e uriaș, iar varietatea de vehicule este absurdă — supercar-uri, muscle cars, off-road beasts, mașini clasice, prototipuri, literalmente tot ce vrei.  Cursele sunt rapide, satisfăcătoare și incredibil de spectaculoase. Poți face drift prin orașe, rally prin păduri sau sprint-uri pe autostradă cu 400 km/h. Jocul te lasă să faci aproape orice.  Puncte Forte Lume open-world magnifică și extrem de variată. Grafică aproape fotorealistă. Gameplay arcade perfect echilibrat între realism și distracție. Sute de mașini cu sunete și handling excelent. Multiplayer distractiv și foarte activ. Conținut enorm și actualizări constante. Puncte Slabe Structura festivalului poate deveni repetitivă după multe ore. AI-ul adversarilor are momente ciudate și uneori „trișează”. Povestea și personajele sunt forgettable — clar nu pentru asta joci. Pentru veteranii seriei, formula începe să fie foarte familiară. Concluzie  Forza Horizon 5 este unul dintre cele mai bune jocuri racing făcute vreodată. Un sandbox auto gigantic, superb și incredibil de distractiv, care îți oferă libertatea totală de a conduce ♥♥♥ vrei, unde vrei și cu ce vrei.  E genul de joc pe care îl pornești „pentru o cursă” și te trezești după 4 ore făcând drift pe un vulcan în timp ce asculti muzică și depășești un Lamborghini cu un Ford vechi tunat absurd.  Pur și simplu… fun. Așa ar trebui să fie orice joc cu mașini. 🚗🔥

Better late than never - I finally got to try a Forza Horizon game just a month before the next one comes out. The good news is that the game remains playable (for now) and is almost certainly in a much better place than at launch, as is the frustrating triple-a way these days. Seasonal challenges and special unlockable content have been given special access and constant rotation in order to make most content accessible with just a bit of grinding races. And "grinding" is probably a terrible word here because...WOW!  This game puts its best foot forward and rarely takes its foot off the gas pedal...erm, pardon the pun. Gorgeous graphics, impeccable audio design, fantastic soundtrack filled with banger after banger, and fantastic addicting racing somewhere between a racing sim and an arcade racer. Playground Games masterfully ballanced approachability for casuals with detail and challenge for hardcores. For context, I'm not "a car guy" but I've always loved the aesthetic of cool cars and racing culture, plus I love racing games. I watch Top Gear and The Grand Tour for the adventure and maybe to learn a little something, not to memorize the technical details. The game will let you dive deep and customize your cars to such an absurd degree that a true "car guy" could be deeply satisfied, or you can handily auto-upgrade at the touch of a button for schmoes like me.  Tons of single-player content, a seemingly welcoming online community, and a presentation that's all about good vibes. Forza Horizon 5 is an excellent escape from reality - its interpretation of Mexico is absolutely gorgeous and filled with varied environments and towns. Oh, Playground, please give a raise to whoever pitched the idea to have multiple races down the side of an active volcano. It's absurd and ridiculous and over-the-top and I wouldn't have it any other way!!  To nitpick a bit, I never quite hit that 5/5 "loving it" feeling. It's still rough around the edges in spots including the mildly horrifying character models and some buggy missions that seem to require you to manually cap your framerate to 60 on PC to even stand a chance to win (wtf??) and some missions that like to disappear until you reboot the game. And any game that integrates DLC into the base game and doesn't clearly label it as DLC until you try to play it, then pulls the ol' "Oopsie poopsie! Swipe your credit card to use that first!" message loses a lot of credit from me - extremely immersion breaking and annoying. And the "story" is just fine. Most of it is running various missions where you get to learn some interesting trivia about Mexican culture and/or car culture. It's interesting, but the dialogue and a lot of the voice acting has me deeply concerned for this studio's upcoming narrative-heavy RPG, Fable. I'll pray to any god who will listen for that project to use different writers than this one. But if you know not to take it seriously, it's mostly harmless.  Ultimately I'm so happy I finally got around to this series I've been meaning to get into for years now. FH6 looks fantastic too, and I plan to go back to at least try FH4 as well. It's a damn shame they can't work out a better deal to extend licenses and keep these on sale indefinitely. I highly recommend buying this before it inevitably gets delisted. I feel like this could be a game I'd come back to again and again, and there's certainly enough cars to collect to be playing for a long time to come.

Overall, I think Forza Horizon is a really enjoyable game that can keep you entertained for a very long time. The cars feel fantastic to drive, and the individual races are a lot of fun — especially the off-road tracks, where you can really feel the terrain. The selection of cars is also huge, and there are plenty of customization options. The game world is varied (forests, deserts, mountains, cities, etc.) and fun to explore.  However, there are also a few downsides, which I’d like to list below:  1) The requirement to have a Microsoft account, the unnecessary and out-of-place casino-style wheel-spin UI when winning new cars, and the challenge cards prominently displayed on the map that cannot be hidden — which are not part of the base game (and must therefore be purchased first) — really rubbed me the wrong way. 2) The constant chatter of the unlikable characters against an overly colorful backdrop sometimes makes the game world feel pretty generic. As for the radio stations, I often wished there were more customization options because the music selection just wasn’t really my thing. I often preferred to just turn the radio off. 3) As much fun as it is to drive around, the game really should have a free fast-travel option on a map this big. And when it comes to starting a race, you still have to sit through several layers of loading and cutscenes that I really wish I could skip more often. 4) The game constantly tries to push you toward certain activities (for example by repeatedly opening the mission map), even though the game is supposed to be all about player freedom. Some level of guidance is fine, but this kind of constant nudging really got on my nerves. 5) There was no German voiceover for the Donut missions. There’s also a strange vehicle-related glitch that I couldn’t explain. Sometimes the car just refuses to accelerate past a certain speed, or it won’t move forward at all, even though the road is flat with no obstacles and the car was previously at a standstill. 6) Some challenges/races seemed impossible for me to complete. For example, you're supposed to reach a certain speed on a stretch of beach within a set time limit, but the car suddenly refuses to accelerate any further at that spot, no matter what you do. Elsewhere, certain opponents gain all sorts of advantages, such as sudden, extreme speed boosts out of nowhere, or the ability to take shortcuts or navigate even the tightest turns without slowing down, while your own vehicle gets artificially slowed down. I found that kind of thing frustrating.

As we're heading to Horizon Festival's next destination, I feel like I should say a few words about this game before hopping behind the wheel of my Lancer VI for the last time in Mexico.   I made acquaintance with the Forza series from Forza Motorsport 4 on my second-hand Xbox360 back in the day. It was brilliant. Hugging apexes in roaring Ferraris, drifting high in the alps in JDM classics - it was new, fresh, and bloody well done.   The same feeling carried over to Horizon. Road racing, hugging tight corners with your loyal beast purring underneath you, pulling insane G's. Drifting, late night sessions with the boys, pushing each other into walls because none of you knew how to properly drift. With an addition of... offroad (excluding Horizon 1), exploring the map in 1,000 horsepower buggies and SUV's while listening to fast-paced Drum & Bass. Playground Games did a damn good job with Horizon 3 and 4, being my all-time favorite Forza games.   But Horizon 5? There are good and bad things about it. Can't complain, overall experience was amazing. Heart-stopping near misses, clean and dirty overtakes, PvP and PvE racing with little kids trying to push you off the track or ram you into walls - it was fun, generally.  Generally.  My main complaint is how barren the map feels. Don't get me wrong, I have countless laps around the whole map of Mexico in my Lancer, with tight corners and long straights diversifying the experience. It's just that the middle of the map feels empty. Same feel, despite where you drive. Vast fields, tight roads, little huts scattered around the land. It was not enough. It still felt empty and uneventful. As if the whole map was designed around the Battle Royale mode, which, let's admit it, was a flop.   The City. It felt rural. For a major city on the map it felt just ancient. Empty. Small. Suffice it to say that after completing every single race in that area I never even considered driving around the city [i] just because [/i]. Simple as that. I have high hopes for Tokyo, and I am very excited to drift through the neon-filled streets of a MODERN city, just like in Horizon 3.   Car Sounds.  Now, pardon me. This section is going to be pretty short, as I have just one major complaint. Why in the ♥♥♥♥ are they re-using sounds for the same car brand over and over again? Lambos and Ferraris sound the EXACT same no matter the model.  Overall..  The game is great. Late-night drives solo or with friends, competing for the first place with randoms whose ego urges them to push you off the course, custom-tuning your cars to your liking, racing through the vast landscapes with Hospital Records blasting fast-paced tunes in your ear and the engine of your AMG GT R roaring like a wild beast beneath you - all those granted me plenty of good memories, fun moments and an overall great impression of the game despite its flaws.  Rating: 7.5/10.   I'll see you in Japan, fellow drivers. Let's race, clean and dirty, for one to emerge victorious!

Forza Horizon 5 takes the foundation of its predecessor and refines it into the ultimate celebration of car culture, moving the festival to the vibrant, sprawling landscapes of Mexico. It doesn’t try to reinvent the wheel. Instead, it focuses on scale, spectacle, and a much more cinematic sense of discovery.  The first thing that hits you is just how gorgeous the game is. Even half a decade after its release, it remains a technical benchmark for the genre. Though it’s a bit of a bittersweet realization knowing my current PC probably won't be able to handle the jump to Horizon 6. The map is a massive part of that beauty. While some players felt it lacked elevation, I didn’t find that to be the case at all. The world has its highs and lows, pun intended, from the towering volcano to the coastal flats. And while the seasons are admittedly less dramatic than the snowy UK winters of the last game, that simply comes with the territory, pun intended again. It’s a natural trade-off for such a diverse Mexican setting.  Where the game truly steps up is in its presentation of the races themselves. In many open-world racers, tracks feel like empty streets with a few arrows taped to a pole, but here, every race feels like a physical event. When you arrive, the track is built out with grandstands, professional start-finish lines, and festival branding. It feels like a real, organized competition. The coolest part is that once the race is over, all that infrastructure is gone, and the road returns to being a normal highway. It adds a layer of immersion that makes the world feel alive.  The progression system remains largely the same as the fourth game, which is great for those who value their time, but it does introduce some smart improvements. The new Expeditions are a highlight. These are scripted, objective-based journeys that act as gateways to new festival sites. They give the game a better sense of pacing and make expanding the festival feel like a genuine milestone rather than just ticking off a checklist.  Of course, the core of the experience is still the cars. There is an insane amount of them to choose from, and they all look, sound, and drive exceptionally well. At the end of the day, Forza Horizon 5 isn't trying to be a grueling simulation. It’s a masterclass in pure, accessible fun. It’s a near-perfect refinement of the formula that makes you feel like the star of the show from the moment you hit the gas.  This ties into the game's greatest strength. The power fantasy. You are treated like absolute royalty from the jump. You can miss your braking point, scrape every wall, and crash through every corner, yet the commentators and fans still treat you like a god-tier superstar. It’s a pure, guilt-free power fantasy that prioritizes your enjoyment over punishing your mistakes. Even when your driving is less than professional, the game refuses to break the illusion that you are the greatest to ever do it.  As for the post-launch content, the two big DLCs: Hot Wheels and Rally Adventure, are both high-quality additions with plenty of content. They are objectively good expansions that offer a lot of variety, though if I’m being honest, I personally fancied the ones in Horizon 4 a bit more. There was just something about the atmosphere of Fortune Island and the charm of LEGO Valley that felt a bit more special to me, even if the Mexico expansions are technically more polished.  It’s a shame the game is still often perceived as a mixed bag by some. For me, it was a great game while it lasted, offering a masterclass in pure, accessible fun. But with the community's eyes already turning toward the future and the hopes of Japan, it feels like it’s finally time for the series to move on.   Unfortunately, because of my hardware, I won’t be joining that next trip. For now, I’m happily stuck in Mexico, and there are far worse places to be stranded.

[h1]Forza Horizon 5: A masterpiece that’s always there for you[/h1]  Forza Horizon 5 is more than just a racing game; it’s an absolute [b]masterpiece[/b]. What I love most is how it fits literally any mood. Whether you're feeling down, stressed, or just pure joy — this game takes you as you are. You can just hop in, start driving, and let the world wash over you. It’s like a digital comfort zone.  [h2]Mexico & The Vibe[/h2] Setting the game in Mexico was such a [u]perfect call[/u]. The map is incredibly immersive and just beautiful to look at. And man, the music... the main menu theme alone is something I could listen to for hours. It sets the vibe perfectly before you even turn the key.  [h2]The Details Matter[/h2] You can really tell the devs poured their hearts into the technical side: [list]     [*][b]Engine Sounds:[/b] Each of the [b]900+ cars[/b] sounds unique. I love how the exhaust note changes depending on your surroundings — the way it echoes when you blast through a tunnel is just spot on.     [*][b]Total Freedom:[/b] The game never tells you "no." Want a high-speed street race? Go for it. Feeling like some rally or off-roading? It’s all there. Want to weave through traffic or just chill and explore the map? [i]The choice is always yours.[/i] [/list]  [h2]The Downsides...[/h2] However, the game isn't perfect, and there are a couple of things that break the immersion: [list]     [*][b]The "Ghost Town" Feeling:[/b]  Despite how beautiful Mexico is, the map often feels [i]empty[/i]. The cities are ghost towns with almost no pedestrians, and the traffic is way too thin. Sometimes you can drive for miles without seeing another soul, which makes the world feel a bit lifeless at times.     [*][b]Lack of Progression:[/b] Because the game constantly showers you with cars and rewards, [b]nothing feels earned anymore[/b]. You don't really build a bond with your cars because they're just handed to you like candy. It loses that "soul" when everything is given to you right away. [spoiler]Supposedly, they’re fixing the progression in FH6 — we’ll have to wait and see.[/spoiler] [/list]  [h1]Verdict[/h1] Even with these flaws, the [i]Forza Horizon[/i] series is easily the best in the business right now. It’s a world you just want to keep coming back to!  [b]Highly recommended![/b]

Forza Horizon 5 is a visually impressive racing game, but it’s not without its flaws.  At first glance, the game looks amazing. The graphics are top-tier, with detailed cars and beautiful lighting. Driving feels smooth and responsive, and there’s a huge variety of cars to choose from. If you enjoy racing mechanics alone, the game definitely delivers.  However, one of the biggest downsides is the map. The game is set in Mexico, and while it sounds interesting on paper, in practice it feels a bit bland. Large parts of the map look very similar, with a lot of empty space and not enough variety to keep things exciting. Compared to previous entries, the environment just doesn’t feel as memorable.  The overall action also feels weaker. Events can become repetitive, and there’s less of that “wow” factor that keeps you constantly engaged. It sometimes feels like you’re just driving around without a strong sense of purpose.  On the positive side, there’s still a lot of content, and the game runs very well. Multiplayer and seasonal events add some replay value, but they don’t fully fix the core issue with the map and overall excitement.  In the end, Forza Horizon 5 is a solid racing game with great visuals and mechanics, but the uninspiring map and weaker sense of action hold it back from being truly amazing.  Rating: 6/10 Forza horizon 4 better

Forza Horizon 5 is a polished game with great graphics and satisfying controls. There is no denying that it is very well made and offers a plethora of activities and races. There are a number of issues nonetheless: the open-world proposed here is less interesting than in Forza Horizon 4, and though it is nice to be able to drive around an open world, it makes specific races very generic. The different types of races are distinct, but individual races tend to blend into one another. There are bugs that can potentially prevent completionists from achieving 100%. Time-gated activities are a nuisance. The dialogues are just as corny as in the previous game.  But the two main reasons I'm giving this a thumbs-down without the slightest hesitation is that (1) the developers must stop trying to force online play and social features down the throat of players who don't want it; and (2) a game that is not free-to-play should never heavily advertise or taunt players with DLC-locked content. The map is littered with markers for activities, with no clear indication as to which is player-created or which is behind a paywall. The in-game autoshow where you buy cars has DLC-paywalled cars in the middle of those you can get normally from the game mechanics. These deleterious aspects of modern games really needed to die out yesterday.

Look, racing games are exactly what you expect. Drive between point a & point b typically as fast as possible, with various modes or event types adding layers of nuance. I grew up on the genre, with my dad always supplying the house with Mario Kart & Need for Speed games. That core block of Underground - Carbon (plus Pro Street for myself) is really the basis for a lot of my preferences with racing games, and as time went on, the Need for Speed series seem to have either drifted away from the core premise that kept me stuck to the series (likely ushered by the decline in car culture come the 2010s), or lost the polish that I felt the games once had compared to others. After Pro Street, I mostly fizzled out on racing games until a few years back having picked up FH4 on a decent Steam discount, serving as my introduction to the series.  To me, Forza Horizon 5 really takes what was already there in 4, and cranks the polishing up to 11 with further refinement in visual and audio fidelity. This game looks & sounds fantastic, it's consistently one of the games that Microsoft uses to showcase hardware (and for good reason.) The map feels huge & densely packed, especially in the more jungle-like areas. But, simultaneously flat & empty as most of the map decoration "budget" appears to go towards flora, and while hilly, the areas feel like they're in their own contained little bubbles (as in, hills are in the "hilly area" and not really in other sections of the map.) The urban environments, while in scale do appear larger then what 4 has to offer, feels invisible the way that it's tucked into a valley. Beyond the map, the narrative is absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The narrative has absolutely zero level of friction, coming across as a luke warm delivery for another reason to just hop in the car and drive fast. And don't get me wrong, I know what genre I'm playing— I don't expect really much in terms of a narrative. But the writing here feels like it is the absolute bare minimum they could get away with. Undoubtedly one of the weakest elements of the game. Beyond that, I sort of despise the lack of "CaRPG" elements that are present in prior mentioned Need for Speed games. Starting out with a beater that you race, upgrade, trick out and eventually buy up into higher classes of cars with introduces some layer of progression to these style of games that I think brings a little spice to the game. Instead, Forza Horizon 5 just hands out cars like candy, and you can run 90% of the game in some super car if you really want to. I understand the accessibility to cars is a turn on for some people, but for me personally, that stuff should wait until "end game" where you've gained some rep as a racer.  My complaints are mostly minute though, and are moreso issues with the delivery of the systems. The game at the end of the day is pretty fun & enjoyable, even if it makes me roll my eyes at times (especially when they just substitute Spanish words in the writing seemingly at random. Do Spanish speakers actually enjoy this?) Driving around in my car of choice is, for the vast majority of the time, a really slick and polished experience. Otherwise, I wouldn't have chased 3 stars on everything on the map.   If you have any interest in cars or racing games, Forza Horizon 5 is a great, approachable game that I'm sure you'll enjoy. 6 looks to be a really exciting entry as well, I presume it'll probably mechanically be very similar.

Overview After 134 hours with Forza Horizon 5, it is clear this is a game that knows how to keep you hooked. It is smooth, polished, and easy to enjoy, but the longer you play, the more certain cracks start to show beneath the surface.  Pros  Visually Impressive World Mexico looks stunning. The environments are varied, from deserts and jungles to coastlines, and everything is detailed and well crafted. From a visual standpoint, it is hard to complain. Driving Feels Just Right The handling is where the game really shines. It is accessible without being boring, and whether you are racing seriously or just cruising, it feels consistently good. Massive Car Collection There is a huge range of vehicles to choose from. You are never really short on options, and experimenting with different builds keeps things interesting. Freedom in Gameplay You are not forced into anything. You can race, explore, tune, or just drive around. That flexibility makes it easy to pick up anytime. Long Lasting Appeal Even after 134 hours, it still has moments that pull you back in. The core gameplay loop is strong enough to hold attention over time.  Cons  World Feels Empty Over Time While the map looks beautiful, it can start to feel lifeless. Outside of events, there is not much happening dynamically, which makes long drives feel a bit hollow after a while. Repetitive Event Structure Many races and challenges start blending into each other. You notice the repetition more the longer you play. Weak Story Presence The story is minimal and forgettable. It does not add much to the overall experience. Online Inconsistencies Multiplayer is not always reliable. Connection issues and matchmaking problems can take away from the experience. AI Balance Issues The AI can feel uneven, either too easy or oddly difficult at times. Underwhelming Engine Sounds A noticeable drawback. Many cars lack distinct, powerful sound profiles, which takes away from the immersion, especially for a car focused game.  Final Verdict Forza Horizon 5 gets the fundamentals right, driving, visuals, and accessibility, but it does not always maintain depth in the long run. It is a great game to jump into, but over time, the emptiness of the world and repetition start to stand out. Still, if you enjoy open world racing, it is worth experiencing.

Форза 4 это одна из лучших релизов этой франшизы, если не лучшая, так как там идеально практически все, от огромнейшего автопарка ( чем эта часть не обделена ), до окружения, детализации и графики, так как в сравнении с предыдущей частью скачек в графическом дизайне значительный, в то время между 4-й и 5-й разница практически незаметна.     В 5-й форзе было странным выбрать жаркую и сухую Мексику после Британии. В Британии заметна смена климата, постоянные дожди и густые туманы весной и осенью, огромное количество снега зимой, и умеренно теплое лето. Странная прогрессия. Получить гиперкар класса S2, можно буквально в первые часы игры, в то время как у стариков NFS это было бы табу. НЕТ.  Форза 5 это все ещё та игра, которая дает на клыка NFS, The Crew и прочих. Игра, к которой должны стремится все разработчики автосимов и аркадных гонок, ведь именно на Playground Games держится вся уникальность Форзы, отличающая её от других игр жанра. The driving feels more natural and responsive, especially during high‑speed turns or off‑road sections. I’m still working out how to map manual shifting to the paddle or quick‑action buttons, but for anyone playing on the easier difficulty settings, automatic transmission works perfectly well while you get your bearings. Despite the learning curve and the sheer volume of things to do, the game shines as a joyful, fast‑paced open‑world racer. After almost 300 hours I honestly can very much recommend this game  The driving itself is honestly the strongest point of this game in my opinion, it perfectly balances itself between a sim and an arcade, which makes sense cos this is a simcade. You are a superstar from the start and you are famous and stuff, it's just not interesting   Also an issue that was pretty big to a lot of PC and Steam players is the fact this game requires a Microsoft account that sadly can sometimes be a real pain to log into. As someone who grew up playing the Forza franchise, this review is going to be a little biased. The short and sweet is, do not start with this game if you're trying to get into Horizon. I would start with either Horizon 1, 4, or 6 once that comes out. All the issues I have with this game are entirely progression based, with the game feeling too easy. It's too easy to get super cars, with you just being given one for free pretty early on. In Horizon 1, you'd have to grind for tens of hours before you even get ONE. In the first couple hours of this game, you get several for nearly free. It kinda trivializes all the early races, and makes the main story feel more bland in my opinion. Thankfully it sounds like they're moving away from that in Horizon 6.  The story is alright, it's a Forza game. The story doesn't have to be good. You do play as a British person tho, so that takes away points from me. Being able to see parts of Mexican car culture is great, though. That's the one thing this game does do really well. It does feel kinda sensationalized, but the point is to celebrate Mexico so it makes sense.  Other than that, the game is REALLY good. The controls are amazing, and honestly the best they've ever been. The game is very pretty despite the really basic map. The music is always amazing in a Forza Horizon game, actually added songs to my playlist from this game. A lot of the models are reused unfortunately, but that's not a terrible thing if you're here for gameplay.  It's definitely one of the weaker entries in the series, but it's still a great game made by amazing developers. 7/10

The car roster is massive and diverse, featuring plenty of 90s Japanese and European icons that are perfect for those who love that specific era’s aesthetic. Beyond the solo content, it’s a fantastic social experience. Cruising in a convoy with a partner or a group of friends turns the game into a digital road trip, whether you're tackling high-stakes races or just exploring the minimalist beauty of the desert at sunset.  It’s polished, joyful, and easily the best "hangout" game currently available.

Forza Horizon 5 is a well-made open-world racing game that offers a lot of content and a great overall experience. The game is set in Mexico, and the map is large and varied, with everything from deserts and jungles to cities and coastlines. The visuals are a standout, and the changing weather helps keep races feeling fresh.  The driving is smooth and easy to get into, but still has enough depth for players who want to tune and customise their cars. There’s a huge range of vehicles to choose from, and each one feels a bit different, which keeps things interesting.  However, the game isn’t perfect. After a while, the races and events can start to feel repetitive, and there isn’t much of a story to keep you engaged. If you’ve played previous Forza Horizon games, this one might feel quite similar, rather than something completely new.  Online features are a nice addition, but they can be inconsistent at times, with occasional connection issues. The soundtrack is decent, but can get repetitive during longer sessions, and some players may not like the focus on paid DLC.  Overall, Forza Horizon 5 is a polished and enjoyable racing game with a lot to offer, even if it doesn’t change much from earlier titles. It’s a solid choice for both casual players and racing fans.

I really wanted to like Forza Horizon 5, but after around 90 hours, I honestly can’t recommend it. While it looks good on the surface, the overall experience feels like a step back compared to Forza Horizon 4 in several important areas.  To start with some positives, the graphics are nice—clean, colorful, and well-optimized—but nothing groundbreaking for a modern title. The photo mode is also genuinely enjoyable and one of the better features of the game if you like capturing your cars in different environments. Another decent addition is the inclusion of Donut Media content, which adds a bit of variety, although it’s still nothing particularly special in the long run.  That said, the negatives quickly outweigh the positives. The sound design is a clear downgrade. Many cars sound worse than they did before, especially VW and Audi 5-cylinder engines (Golf R32, Audi Quattro, RS3, RS2, etc.), along with several Porsche models. Overall, a large portion of the cars have very generic engine sounds, which seriously hurts immersion.  The Mexico map looks beautiful, but it feels completely lifeless. Roads are often empty, and many areas repeat the same patterns. After some time, everything starts to feel dull, and there’s very little that keeps exploration interesting or rewarding.  Customization is another weak point. Car customization feels almost identical to Horizon 4, if not slightly worse in some cases. On top of that, character customization is extremely limited and dull—you can’t really create your driver the way you want, only the way the game allows you to. For a newer title, this lack of evolution is disappointing.  The backstage and auction systems are frustrating and unnecessarily restrictive. If you want specific cars like a 911 GT3 RS (2023) or a GR Yaris, you’re forced into grinding or paying for passes and points. Even worse, after all that effort, the car might not even feel as good as you expected.  The monetization model is also unacceptable. Even if you buy the Ultimate or Premium Edition, you still have to pay extra for additional car packs. That completely defeats the purpose of those editions. Cars like multiple GT3 variants or something like a Golf 8R should have been included as free updates, not locked behind extra payments. It feels like a clear cash grab.  The “career” or story mode is another major disappointment. It feels like a failed attempt at creating something meaningful, but in reality, it’s shallow and completely pointless. There’s no real sense of progression or engagement—it’s just there without adding anything valuable to the experience.  The Hot Wheels expansion is also underwhelming. It’s decent, but nothing memorable. Compared to the LEGO expansion from Horizon 4, it feels like a downgrade in creativity and fun.  Overall, despite having a huge number of cars, the game lacks real substance. Within about 50 hours, you’ve pretty much seen everything it has to offer. After that, there’s little motivation to keep playing, as the world doesn’t pull you back in and the gameplay loop becomes repetitive.  It’s disappointing, especially considering how high expectations were. In the end, this feels like one of the weakest Horizon titles so far.

On a technical level, this is a good game. You will have a good time  But it's worse than FH3 and FH4 in many ways. Sadly you can't buy those anymore (and they were never on steam), so this is a decent first entry for anyone interested in the FH series on steam. I'm recommending it for that alone  - The map is really bland and generic - the locations from Mexico are beautiful but the actual road feel of racing through these locations lacks variety. I still find myself booting up FH3 / FH4 if I want to just drive around and vibe. I can't stress enough how much this harms the game because it affects every aspect of the game - the tracks, the driving around for fun, or just driving to the next event - Song selection is quite hit or miss - there's some really good ones mixed in with some mediocre ones, which is a shame given how good the song selection has been (dare I say) iconic in the previous games. Another big hit to the feel of the game because Horizon is basically a music festival with cars - Some cars are gatekept behind weekly chores and if you miss them you have to grind ridiculous amounts of credits to auction snipe them. Honestly introducing this in FH4 was a mistake and I feel they should remove it for FH6 - Later on they added car pack DLCs but it feels like they kind of just gutted the car collection from FH4 just to drip feed it through the weekly chores (see above) and to resell the remaining later after people complained about weekly chores. So the way to get cars beyond the initial collection is to grind with time and pay with money - Story makes no sense because you aren't working your way up in the world anymore, somehow you just have access to high end cars immediately which can be a plus for some people but it causes the game to lack direction - Depiction of mexicans in the game is really cringe because they do this spanglish thing where they keep inserting random spanish words into english dialogue. Either give us normal english (which mexicans are capable of speaking) or mexican dialogue with english subs. The spanglish just feels culturally inappropriate - Lack of mexican car culture in general - other than 1 sidequest and a few references, the game doesn't celebrate the region's car culture as much as previous games. I enjoyed learning about how the beetle was called 'vocho' and how it's beloved in Mexico but that's about it. In general Mexico just felt like flavor of the week dripped onto a generic Horizon game, instead of an opportunity to let all of us in the rest of the world to experience their culture through the game. It's not a net negative but it's huge missed potential

[h3]Forza Horzion 5, it’s fun, it’s chaotic, but prepare for an overwhelming amount of content[/h3]   For brief context, I’ve played every Forza Motorsport game from 1 all the way through to 8, but I have only played Horizon 1 and 2. Safe to say that jumping into Horizon 5 was wild. From the very first second, you’re dropped out of a plane into loud music, massive jumps, and cars being gifted to you left, right, and center.   It’s a huge contrast to Forza Motorsport, which starts calm, measured, and almost meditative. Horizon 5 immediately throws you into action, and honestly, it’s fun, both to race and just to drive around freely. But at the same time, it can feel a little confusing and exhausting with just how much is going on.   [h2]The Good[/h2]   Firstly, and most importantly, The driving is fun and easy. Coming from Forza Motorsport, I can feel the difference when using a controller. Horizon is more arcade-like, but not ridiculously so. Cars feel distinct, off-road and on-road handling is satisfying, and tuning makes a real difference in car handling. The showcase events like racing a train or racing three jet skis are insane but thrilling.   The number of cars available is also insane with over 900 cars. Hypercars, hatchbacks, forgotten relics, trucks, lorries, rally cars, you name it. I’ve driven everything from a parade float to a tiny micro car that can only fit one person, to a JDM legend like the Nissan Skyline, to a 1000hp hypercar like the Koenigsegg. After 30 hours, I have about 150 cars as it’s extremely easy to acquire cars in this game (more on that later) and that’s only scratching the surface. The variety here is unmatched. This game is easily the best I’ve ever played in terms of the number of cars on offer.  But let’s talk about the world that Horizon is set in; Mexico is huge and varied, beaches, jungles, mountains, deserts, airfields, winding villages. The game encourages exploration, and even though the streets feel mostly empty and NPCs sit behind invisible walls, it’s still fun to cruise around and discover things.   In terms of the Graphics and the audio, they are both very nice, lighting through the trees looks great and I find the engine sounds to be pretty good (although not perfect). Weather effects are cool in theory while driving around but can be inconsistent (rain suddenly stops in seconds). Music is mostly ignorable if you just want engine sounds, but including a classical radio station this time is hilarious.  One last positive that I want to mention, Forza is known for being impressively inclusive, during the character customisation, you can add prosthetic limbs, you can add hearing aids, and putting your male character in a dress is hilarious, but I guess it’s also good inclusivity. Also, the game calling you by your own name is a nice touch.   [h2]The Bad[/h2]   My main issue is going to seem strange to some, but it’s to do with the amount of content in Horizon 5, There’s so much. Hundreds of races, thousands of accolades, hundreds of cars to collect, collectibles to find on the map, and festival playlists to complete weekly and monthly.  At first, it’s very confusing, I didn’t know for a while what I was supposed to be doing. Accolades come for literally everything, sometimes completely random and if you are trying to do everything 100%? Well, that feels like a monumental task, possibly taking hundreds or even thousands of hours.  Also, the progression feels hollow. Being gifted dozens of cars in the first few hours is fun, but it removes the sense of achievement you get from working your way up from old, slow cars to a hypercar, maybe I just miss the days of old racing games that force you to work your way up so once you finally get round to driving a Ferrari or Lamborghini, you really feel like you’ve earned it.  I personally would have preferred a slower, earned progression.  But in terms of story… Well… What story? Honestly, it’s just an excuse for racing. Dialogue is cringey (looking at you, Ramiro), forgettable, and mostly unneeded. The game likes to remind you that you are in Mexico by throwing in a totally random Spanish word into the dialogue like “amigo”. Also there seemed to be many references to Horizon 4 that went over my head because I never played it.  The map itself, while varied, has nothing in it that really stands out. There’s no open city, only a tiny village with tight roads. Streets are mostly empty; NPCs are behind invisible walls. The world feels more like a showcase sandbox than a living place.  And finally, if you are someone that like me that likes to get achievements, well… be prepared for a gigantic task ahead, because in Horizon 5 the achievements are ridiculously grindy, especially online achievements involving game modes like The Eliminator. Winning The Eliminator feels like a mix of luck and excessive map knowledge.   Also, some festival playlist achievements require waiting weeks or maybe even months for challenges to appear. Maybe that’s fun for hardcore fans of the game, but exhausting for anyone else.   [h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]   I’m about 30 hours in and have finished the main Hall of Fame “story.” Now it’s a do-whatever sandbox, which can feel freeing but also overwhelming. For me, Horizon 5 is best for casual players and car enthusiasts. If you enjoy driving, exploring, and trying cars without feeling pressured to complete everything then this game is going to be a 10/10 for you, one of the best out there. But for Hardcore racers or achievement hunters this might feel exhausting.  Horizon 5 is fun, engaging, occasionally overwhelming, but it’s memorable, so it's worth a go, even if Ramiro is one of the cringiest “Amigos” I’ve ever come across in a game  [h3] RATING: 7.6/10[/h3]

O meta do jogo é montar carros que enganem o sistema que julga a classe do carro (PI). Assim, os melhores carros nas partidas online são justamente aqueles que o PI considera os piores do jogo. Por isso você vai ver que o carro meta de rally é um AMG CLK GTR, um supercarro de pista, que os tuners adaptam para ser bom na terra. Porém o sistema de PI acha, com razão, que esse carro seria horrível na terra por ser um carro de pista. Isso gera uma situação em que os carros que ficam sempre no pódio são os mais bizonhos do jogo, que não fazem sentido no contexto da corrida.  Swap AWD. A transmissão AWD é muito OP no jogo, pois ela é mais rápida, e os tuners usam barras antitorção e ajustes no diferencial para anular o understeer natural da tração 4x4. Isso gera uma situação em que praticamente todos os carros da sua garagem acabam tendo swap AWD, o que mata a diversidade entre os carros.  Falta de progressão e sensação de conquista.

First of all, I want to say that despite many of the things I’ll mention below, I actually like Forza Horizon 5 in some ways. The game gives me a kind of semi-meditative experience ("semi" because you still need to keep an eye on the road): driving at full speed down long roads while enjoying the game’s excellent graphics creates a very pleasant, almost relaxing vibe. The atmosphere can be genuinely enjoyable.  That said, many of us grew up on games like NFS, where each story begins with you being a nobody in a Ford Focus, surrounded by cool racers, and your entire journey is about proving yourself. Compared to that, the atmosphere in Forza – where you’re already the center of the universe, a superstar invited to the festival, and everyone constantly reminds you how amazing you are – feels more like a racing fantasy with unicorns. Many players don’t really like this approach, and I personally feel quite skeptical about it as well.  The racing itself, with default settings, is also fairly easy. Even on higher difficulty levels, it’s often enough to overtake everyone early and then just stay on the road (the racing line helps a lot with that). If you make a mistake, you can simply rewind time and try again. The game constantly supports the player in every possible way, sometimes even too much. Of course, no one forces you to use these features, but their presence clearly shows that the focus is on creating a comfortable experience rather than a competitive one. Whether that’s good or bad is up to you.  Maybe playing with a steering wheel, manual transmission, realistic settings, and the highest difficulty would make it much more challenging compared to using a controller with standard assists. But honestly, that kind of experience feels more like what the Motorsport series is designed for rather than Horizon. All of this is largely a matter of taste.  What really disappointed me, however, is the instability of the game. Especially after recent updates, it started crashing regularly (and judging by Steam reviews,  I’m far from the only one). The game just froze and crashed to the desktop without saving any progress. This happens on a modern system that runs this and other modern games without any issues. One of my crashes happened at 99% of a final cross-country race, literally right before the finish line. That’s certainly a memorable experience, but not the kind you expect from a project of this scale. Optimization is a major downside.  [b]To sum it up: the game has excellent graphics, a huge number of cars, and a generally pleasant and friendly vibe. However, the gameplay  design   feels somewhat questionable, repeating the same “Forza conveyor” formula year after year. It kind of works, but it’s also starting to feel stale. The technical issues make it very hard for me to recommend the game despite its strengths. Future entries in the series really need better technical stability and more variety in gameplay, races, and story presentation. As it stands, Forza Horizon 5 is simply too inconsistent for me to recommend it.[/b]

I went the route of Forza Motorsport before Forza 5 in my experience.  Most of what led me to that was others playing it but I was always confused as to why Motorsport got such mixed reviews when I honestly liked what it was for WHAT it was.  Most of my background in similar comes from Gran Turismo, harkening back to the original release on the PlayStation, so MS didn't really strike me as a bad game, per se.  Then I played Forza 5.  I get it now.  They did give up quite a bit for Motorsport.  It's very much like Gran Turismo Sport, in that respect, in terms of similarity for modern day releases.  It's there to be close to the sims whereas Forza 5 has more of a fun, arcade-y feel with a lot more to do for what you buy at a similar price.  If you're even mildly interested in an arcade racer with a lot of options and this fits your budget you should most certainly try it out.  It handles all levels of play and has a wide variety of things to do, whether it's messing with classic cars, messing with more modern, super-powered cars...messing with Lego cars...there's quite a bit to do and experience.  In all honesty, both games have their strengths and I think if you like 5 and you see MS on sale to give that a try if you haven't already, especially if you have a similar background to the above.  Otherwise, maybe wait for 6 to release like I am if having a game close to the sims isn't your thing.

I’ve been playing since the first Forza, and Horizon 5 still manages to feel fresh. The overall experience just keeps getting better each release. The world is fun to explore, the car list is huge, and there’s always something to do whether you feel like racing, cruising, or just messing around.  At first the tuning system, shared setups, and all the different events can feel a bit overwhelming. There’s a lot going on. But once you understand how upgrades and community tunes work, the game really opens up. YouTube guides and shared builds help a lot, and after that it becomes very engaging instead of complicated.  I started on keyboard, then switched to a controller, and later got a Logitech G920 wheel to enjoy the driving more seriously. The wheel definitely feels more immersive, but it’s also much harder to control at first. You actually have to drive properly instead of just steering and flooring it, which makes it more rewarding once you get used to it.  I’m about 89 hours in and still only around a quarter of the achievements done, so there’s clearly a ton of content. It’s one of those games you can casually jump into or grind seriously, and it works both ways.  If you like cars at all, it’s easy to recommend. It respects your time and always gives you something fun to do.
